title: The Golden Deer
hookLine: a golden deer and a cry in Rama's voice: Nyaya's name for a reason that only looks like one
carry: hetvabhasa: a reason that only looks real
tomorrow: a boy at Death's door is offered every treasure. what does he want instead?

cards: In the forest at Panchavati, Sita sees a deer at the edge of the clearing, and it doesn't look like any deer. Its coat is gold, flecked with silver, and it glows. She asks Rama to catch it for her.
Lakshmana, Rama's brother, frowns. No deer like that exists, he says. That's a demon in disguise.
He's right. It's Maricha, sent by Ravana: a shape-shifter wearing a shape too beautiful to resist. Rama goes after it anyway, and leaves Lakshmana to guard Sita.

teach.h: A VOICE THAT SOUNDS LIKE RAMA.
teach.b: Deep in the forest, Rama's arrow finds the deer. And as Maricha dies, he does one last thing. He cries out in Rama's own voice: oh Sita, oh Lakshmana.
Back at the hut, Sita hears it. That's Rama, she thinks, so Rama is in danger. Go!
Lakshmana says nothing can harm his brother. She won't hear it, she speaks to him harshly, and he goes. With the hut unguarded, Ravana steps out of the trees.
That's the Ramayana, and it turns on two things that only looked real: a deer that shone like gold, and a voice that sounded exactly like Rama.
Nyaya has a name for the second kind of trap: hetvabhasa. Hetu is a reason; abhasa is a semblance, something that shines like what it isn't. The Nyaya Sutra lists five.

The first is the wandering reason: a sign that shows up where your conclusion is true, and also where it isn't. Rama's voice crying out shows up when Rama is in danger. It also shows up when a shape-shifter copies him.
So it can't settle anything. Nyaya didn't write about Sita; that's a reading, through its list.
But notice who gets fooled: not a careless person, Sita herself. That's why Nyaya takes this seriously. Its Sutra opens by tying freedom from false knowledge to the highest good.
For this school, checking a reason is spiritual work, because false knowledge is where suffering gets in. Today the voices come by text.

teach.h: DOES IT SHOW UP WHEN NOTHING'S WRONG?
teach.b: Before you run, ask the Nyaya question: does this sign also show up when nothing's wrong?

how: Students of Nyaya learn the hetvabhasas, the kinds of false reason, from the Nyaya Sutra and use them to test arguments with a teacher; many Hindus pray 'asato ma sad gamaya', lead me from the unreal to the real.

a school that distrusts every reason given

games.q: the golden deer, in Nyaya's words — tap the pairs.
p: the demon in a golden deer's shape
a sign that shows up when he's fine too
a reason that only looks like one
a semblance: shines like what it isn't

s: Lakshmana believed the golden deer was real
he warned that no deer like that exists: it was Maricha in disguise.
the Nyaya Sutra lists five kinds of false reason
the hetvabhasas, starting with the wandering reason.
Nyaya checks reasons only to win debates
its Sutra ties freedom from false knowledge to the highest good.

games.q: you hear a cry in a voice exactly like Rama's. by Nyaya, what's wrong with "that's his voice, so he's in danger"?
o: nothing: a voice you know is proof enough.
the reason wanders: that voice also shows up when a shape-shifter copies him.
the reason flips: hearing him proves he's safe.
games.why: a wandering reason shows up where the conclusion is false too. Maricha could copy the voice, so the voice alone couldn't settle it.

practice: Sit with the breath, and bring to mind one because you've believed lately, about someone or about yourself. Say the reason quietly and ask: does this sign also show up when it isn't true? Don't argue with it; just look.

If you pray, there's an old prayer for exactly this, from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad: asato ma sad gamaya, lead me from the unreal to the real. If you don't pray, say: let me see what's really there.

wordCard.voice: Nyaya. Today, hetvabhasa: a reason that only looks like a reason, like a cry that sounds just like Rama.

orig.note: Sanskrit: hetvabhasa, from hetu, a reason, and abhasa, a semblance: a false reason.

carryVoice: Your line: hetvabhasa, a reason that only looks real. Even Sita heard the false voice. Go gently.
